speaker: markalbrechta
text: May it please the Court, Mark Albrecht for the appellants. This is an appeal of the trial court's granting of summary judgment of the appellee's foreclosure complaint. Now, the trial court granted the motion for summary judgment in spite of numerous affirmative defenses asserted by the appellants. The trial court found that there were no general issue of material fact in dispute, and that the appellees refuted and disproved appellant's affirmative defenses, which then entitled the appellees to summary judgment. While the trial court did not state specifically, it seems to have based its granting of the appellee's motion for summary judgment on the principles of caveat emptor, integration and merger, and uncontestability, and on the Billington versus Jen Lapine Island Limited case, which is at 192 Southern 3rd 77, a case from 2016. Appellants asserted numerous affirmative defenses. Some of those included failure of consideration, deceptive and unfair practices, fraudulent inducement, failure to perform, and fraud in the making of the contract and the performance of the contract. There are numerous others as well, but most of them arose out of the fraud that's asserted to have been done by the appellees. Now, appellants submit that the granting of the appellee's motion for summary judgment on the foreclosure complaint was error on factual and legal grounds, and we submit that the summary judgment in this case should be reversed based on the bases that were set forth by this court in McIntosh Fish Camp LLC versus Caldwell at 315 Southern 3rd 784, which was decided by this court last year. We'll call that McIntosh 1. That appeal dealt with the summary judgment granted as to appellants counterclaim against the appellees, and that counterclaim contained many of the same allegations and assertions that are asserted by the affirmative defenses in this case.

speaker: edwards
text: For this summary judgment, did the appellees offer any additional proof to show that there were no genuine issues of material fact, or did they simply rely on their affidavits?

speaker: markalbrechta
text: The affidavits that were submitted by the appellees in this matter merely recited the terms of the agreement, the mortgage, and the note, and that that had not been complied with, and the amounts were due. There were no assertions in any of the summary judgment factually disputing any of the facts that were asserted in the affirmative defenses, as well as in the appellant's affidavit in opposition. So that leads me to the conclusion that it was based purely on legal principle expressed in Billington, and the argument that the contract, since it was an as-is contract, foreclosed any possibility or option legally of asserting those kinds of defenses. We would submit that if the argument that those legal principles do not foreclose the opportunity to raise these affirmative defenses, then their whole rationale and basis for the summary judgment falls apart, because they did submit no factual allegations to contest the allegations made by the appellees. And this court already decided in McIntosh 1 that those legal principles do not prevent the prosecution of a counterclaim based on fraud and misrepresentation in the making of the conduct of the contract, then those legal principles should not invalidate the affirmative defenses asserted by the appellants. So furthermore, if the affirmative defenses are valid pursuant to the principles in McIntosh 1, then the granting of the summary judgment here was error because the appellees did not factually overcome the affirmative defenses asserted. Now, we submit that the Billington case is factually and legally distinguishable from this case. The Billington case, they were concerned about claims based on representations allegedly made outside of the contract. On the other hand, the claims here in these affirmative defenses are based on the contract for sale and purchase itself. Now, the contract language in Billington specifically significantly differs from the language in this case. And the Billington contract has stated that buyer acknowledges that buyer has not relied upon such statements from any such statements, promises, or representations. On the other hand, this contract provides that buyer agrees to rely solely on seller and others for verification of the property conditions, square footage, and facts that materially affect the property value. So this contract...
